assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reached 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, a precision regime that turns atomic structure and laser spectroscopy into a probe of fundamental physics: tests of constancy of constants, gravitational redshift across millimetres, and a route to a redefinition of the second. The magic-wavelength idea is simple, original and decisive. As an atomic theorist I value that this rests on precise atomic-structure calculations and extremely well-controlled systematics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first strontium lattice clock. Ye built the highest-performing clocks and pushed the systematic floor. Two laureates represent the field cleanly. Other groups (e.g., Lemonde, Lisdat, Ludlow/NIST) contributed, so the boundary is not perfectly sharp.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent laboratories (Japan, USA, Germany, France, China) have reproduced and surpassed each other, with direct clock-to-clock comparisons. The interpretation is stable and the work is mature; ion clocks from Wineland's group were already recognised in 2012 and 2005 recognised the comb, so timing is plausible.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as a refinement of already-honoured precision-time work (2005, 2012) rather than a new principle.
The fair share of credit beyond two names (Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Hinkley and others) is uncertain, and I am working from memory rather than verified records.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1995 proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and the later proposals for quantum simulation with cold atoms provided the concrete physical blueprint that turned quantum-information ideas into laboratory programmes. It is original, clear, and has had a lasting effect across AMO physics, linking fundamental quantum mechanics to controllable many-body systems.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller are the evident joint originators of the ion-trap gate proposal and the cold-atom simulator ideas. The credit is compact and unusually clean for a theory prize, with two persons.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally realised and extended by many groups over three decades (ion traps, neutral atoms, Rydberg systems). Confirmation is deep and independent. The 2012 prize to Wineland and Haroche covered the experimental control, so a theory prize is timely and consistent. Recognition is overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers experimental realisations to theory proposals.
The relative weighting of the gate proposal versus the simulation proposals, and the contribution of others such as Kimble or Monroe/Wineland to the gate demonstration, are not settled in my mind.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and the Berry phase reveal that the geometry and topology of the quantum state, not only local forces, determines physical outcomes. This changed how physicists think about gauge potentials, adiabatic evolution and topology in matter, and it underlies the later quantum Hall, topological-phase and polarisation theories. It is exactly the kind of unexpected, fundamental insight I find most compelling.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) together made the original prediction; David Bohm is deceased, so Aharonov alone carries the first idea. Berry (1984) is the clear originator of the geometric phase, with Simon, Pancharatnam and others as precursors. The two credited names are the supportable living pair, although the composite is two discoveries bridged by a common theme.
assessment.maturity: Both effects have been verified experimentally many times (Tonomura electron holography, molecular and optical geometric-phase experiments) and are textbook content. The age of the discoveries and of the principals makes recognition urgent; it is long mature, not premature.
uncertainties: Aharonov-Bohm is a joint discovery with the deceased David Bohm, which complicates the prize configuration.
Whether the committee will treat two separate discoveries as one prize, and the role of Pancharatnam, Simon and Wilczek-Zee in the geometric-phase lineage.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapping, cooling and precision spectroscopy of antihydrogen and of single antiprotons test CPT symmetry and gravity for antimatter. Gabrielse's single-particle trap methods and Hangst's ALPHA trapping and 1S-2S and hyperfine spectroscopy are exceptional, precise measurements that address where the symmetries of nature hold, matching my preference for fundamentally motivated precision work.
assessment.attribution: Gabrielse (Penning-trap methods, antiproton and positron experiments, electron g-factor) and Hangst (ALPHA, first trapped antihydrogen, spectroscopy and gravity) are the two supportable leaders. ATRAP and ALPHA were competing and complementary efforts, and credit within each large collaboration is intertwined; the pairing is fair but not unambiguous.
assessment.maturity: Key results (trapping 2010, 1S-2S 2016, antihydrogen gravity 2023) were confirmed by successive measurements and independent collaborations, but the spectroscopic precision is still far below that of hydrogen, so the fundamental test is not yet decisive. Mature as a method, early as a symmetry test.
uncertainties: No violation of CPT has been seen, so the physical payoff is a limit and not a discovery.
Allocation between ALPHA, ATRAP and ASACUSA/AEgIS groups, and the exact role of Gabrielse's electron g-2 work, are uncertain to me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Controlled interfaces between single photons and atoms or atomic ensembles (cavity QED, EIT-based storage, quantum repeater protocols) turn light-matter coupling into the basic building block for quantum memories and networks. Conceptually clear and widely applied, it extends the 2012 prize for single quantum systems into networks and communication.
assessment.attribution: Kimble (quantum network vision, strong coupling), Rempe (single-atom cavity QED, photon-by-photon control) and Lukin (EIT storage, protocols) are three prominent contributors. Lukin appears in several other topics, and Hau, Duan, Polzik, Gisin and others also have claims; the discovery is a broad programme, not a single event.
assessment.maturity: Elementary quantum memories and elementary network links have been demonstrated by several laboratories, but the field is still maturing toward scalable networks. The key demonstrations are robust; the overarching narrative is still developing.
uncertainties: The topic is broad and the definition of the prize-worthy core is unclear.
Competing credit for EIT-based storage (Hau, Lukin, Phillips) and for quantum repeater work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The three-step recollision picture and its quantum formulation explain high-harmonic generation and form the theoretical base of attosecond science. The simple image, ionise, accelerate in the laser field, recollide, is the kind of intuitive explanation I value, and it lets experiments be interpreted quantitatively. It is the natural theoretical complement to the 2023 prize for the experiments.
assessment.attribution: Corkum (1993 semiclassical model) is most central; Schafer, Kulander and co-workers gave a closely contemporaneous formulation, and Lewenstein et al. gave the 1994 quantum theory. I have a professional connection to this community and to a 2023 laureate and would need to weigh recusal; my ranking here is therefore deliberately cautious.
assessment.maturity: The recollision model is confirmed by a very large body of independent experiments and underlies attosecond metrology and spectroscopy, so it is mature. However, the 2023 prize already honoured attosecond physics and the committee may see this as already largely covered.
uncertainties: Prior recognition in 2023 may count against a further award in the same field.
Priority questions among Corkum, Kulander/Schafer, Krause and Lewenstein, and my own conflicts of interest.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry exploits matter-wave coherence for rotation, gravity and gradient sensing and for tests of the equivalence principle and the fine-structure constant. It carries the wave nature of matter into precision measurement, which bears directly on the boundary between quantum and classical behaviour I find important.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard (first atom interferometer with gratings), Bordé (Ramsey-Bordé interferometer and theory), Kasevich (light-pulse interferometers and applications) are plausible; Chu and Phillips are already laureates for related work, and Ketterle, Mlynek and Keith also contributed, so credit is diffuse.
assessment.maturity: The field is well confirmed by many groups, with commercial and fundamental instruments, but the most decisive fundamental tests are still being improved. The distinction from the 1997 and 2001 recognition may be thin.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier Nobel recognition of laser cooling, BEC and the matter-wave concept.
Diffuse credit among many early contributors.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise Hubbard models, the superfluid-Mott transition and quantum gas microscopy, giving direct, tunable access to strongly correlated quantum matter. It is original, conceptually clear, and has high impact across AMO and condensed-matter physics.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch (with Cirac) proposed the Hubbard-model realisation; Greiner (with Bloch and Hänsch) observed the Mott transition; Bloch built the platform and the microscopes; Esslinger realised fermionic Mott states. Five names are credited and a maximum of three can be selected, so the choice excludes valid contributors, notably Cirac and Esslinger.
assessment.maturity: Extensively reproduced and extended by many groups, with quantum simulation now a mature tool. The overlap in names with the Cirac-Zoller entry reduces the chance that both are recognised in one year.
uncertainties: Which three of the five names best match the decisive contributions, and the omission of Jaksch, who is not in the credited list.
Overlap with the Cirac-Zoller candidate and with the 2001 BEC prize.
